messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Models and %CV
parts:
You cannot use AIC as a comparison across different truncation distances.
It will likely continue to decrease as the truncation increases and as you
noted the CV will increase. You should select a truncation distance and
then use AIC to compare models. You should look at the fit (particularly
near x=0) to evaluate the best truncation distance. You really only want
to truncate if the tail of the distribution is causing a poor fit at the
origin (x=0) and that can cause differences in the density estimates.
--jeff

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Models and %CV
parts:
Sandro:

Here are some quick thoughts about what you present:

Of the cosine vs. polynomial adjustment term contrast you present, there
seems to be evidence to prefer the cosine adjustment terms. You then
show that with truncation and the cosine adjustments you get "better
fit" (you do not quantify what you mean by better fit; did the
untruncated models fit?), but at the loss of some precision. It is not
surprising that you lose some precision as measured by CV (but remember
CV is ratio of SE(DS)/DS); given that your point estimate (DS) decreased
a small bit (7.2 vs 6.7) that may be the explanation for the small rise
in CV.

Two things to keep in mind:
a) it is not necessary to have best fit, only necessary to have models
with adequate fit. Parsimony argues that you should use a model that
only fits your data (and no more); so if your goodness of fit statistic
is acceptable, then stop.

b) you might consider asking Distance not to report the estimates of
density while you are performing your model selection, that way your
decisions about models are not coloured by the estimates models produce.

Finally as Jeff just noted, changing truncation changes data, and AIC
cannot be used for model selection to determine truncation.

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Models and %CV
parts:
It occurred to me that some folks may not quite understand why you can't
compare AICs when you change the data. A more familiar example may help.
First though AIC=-2*log likelihood + 2*number of parameters. The
log-likelihood value is a function of the data and the model/parameters.
With AIC we want to keep the data constant so we can evaluate differences
due to the model/parameters. An example, everyone should know is linear
regression. The log-likelihood for linear regression is a function of the
sum of the squared residuals: (yhat1-y1)^2+(yhat2-y2)^2 + ...+(yhatn-yn)^2
where yhati is the predicted value on the line for the ith observation and
yi is the ith observation. Now consider what happens if I remove or add
another value. Clearly, the sum-of-squared residuals will change (unless
per chance the residual was zero but the likelihood will change because it
includes n). Thus the likelihood value (and thus AIC) will change even if
the model stays the same. Not what you want.

regards --jeff

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Models and %CV
parts:
Chris sent this message to me off-list but I decided to share my answer
with the list.
On Thu, Nov 8, 2012 at 9:07 AM, Chris Merkord <ch...@merkord.com> wrote:

> > Hi Jeff,
> >
> > Your reply to Sandro raised a question for me. How do you judge whether a
> > model has poor fit at the origin? By visually inspecting the density
> > function plotted over a histogram, by looking at the contribution of the
> > first couple of cells of a chi-square goodness of fit test, or something
> > else altogether?
> >
> > Thanks very much for your thoughts.
> >
> >
Both but add into that your understanding of the data field collection and
possibility for measurement error. For example, when I taught a class and
we had them collect data in the field on cactus, I had some come back with
their results and the negative exponential as the best model. I asked them
whether they thought that the probability of detection was lower on on
either side of their foot than it was right between their legs. Now the
negative exponential is an easy target but the point is you should use your
knowledge about the data collection. But usually what I'm describing is
fairly obvious from the plot where the adjustments are trying to fit a long
tail and it clearly doesn't fit well near the origin and either way
undershoots or overshoots the first one or two histogram bins. However,
don't over think things too much and get into the paralysis of analysis.
Well-collected data with a small amount of truncation or covariates that
explain the tail are your best bets with the emphasis on good field data
collection and testing. --jeff
